article_title: Mozilla Rotates Firefox and Thunderbird GPG Signing Key After Accidental GitHub Exposure
summary: Substantively accurate across both sources (BleepingComputer verified via WebFetch fallback), but one quote doesn't match Mozilla's wording and one detailed claim is misattributed to the wrong source.

findings.message: The RPM-specific remediation breakdown (Fedora 43+ vs. Fedora 42/older, RHEL/Rocky/Almalinux, openSUSE/SUSE) is attributed to BleepingComputer ('per BleepingComputer'), but this level of distribution-specific detail is not present in BleepingComputer's article -- it comes from Mozilla's own blog post, which lists exactly this breakdown.
findings.details: Confirmed by reading sources/2026-08/mozilla-rotates-firefox-and-thunderbird-gpg-signing-key-after-accidental-github-exposure/source-0.html.gz (Mozilla's blog) directly, and independently verifying via WebFetch that BleepingComputer's article only says detailed instructions exist without reproducing them.

findings.message: The article quotes Mozilla as saying it has "implemented safeguards to prevent similar incidents." Mozilla's actual wording is: "We have revoked the previous signing key and added safeguards to prevent similar issues in the future." Meaning preserved, wording paraphrased and presented as verbatim.
Source access restricted (bot blocked): HTTP 403, independently verified via WebFetch
findings.details: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/mozilla-updates-gpg-key-for-signing-firefox-thunderbird-releases-after-exposure/ -- no snapshot could be saved, but the claims genuinely attributed to it (the low-risk assessment quote, the manual-verification-steps quote, and the Thunderbird RPM quote) were verified via WebFetch against the live URL and match verbatim.

content_preview.title: Mozilla Rotates Firefox and Thunderbird GPG Signing Key After Accidental GitHub Exposure
content_preview.summary: Mozilla revoked and replaced a GPG signing subkey after an unencrypted copy leaked into a private GitHub repo, finding no evidence of unauthorized use.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Mozilla has rotated the GPG signing subkey it uses to authenticate certain Firefox and Thunderbird release artifacts after discovering that an unencrypted copy of the previous subkey had been accidentally exposed. In a [Mozilla security blog post](https://blog.mozilla.org/security/2026/08/10/updated-gpg-key-for-signing-firefox-and-thunderbird-releases/), the organization said "an unencrypted copy of the previous subkey was inadvertently committed to a private GitHub repository."

editor_notes.content_quality: Concise, well-organized Briefing appropriate to the category's word range. Correctly discloses in 'What We Don't Know' that Mozilla did not specify how long the key was exposed or the audit's scope.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read Mozilla's blog snapshot directly and verified BleepingComputer's claims via WebFetch (403 blocked, no archive.org fallback). Mozilla's blog confirms the exposure quote, the affected-artifacts quote, the audit-finding quote, both key fingerprints, the Aug 5 2028 expiration, and the RPM remediation breakdown by distribution verbatim -- but the RPM breakdown is misattributed to BleepingComputer in the article (see finding), and the 'implemented safeguards to prevent similar incidents' quote doesn't match Mozilla's actual wording (see finding). BleepingComputer (verified via WebFetch) confirms the low-risk assessment quote, the manual-verification-steps quote, and the Thunderbird RPM-exemption quote verbatim.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All facts are directionally accurate; the issues found are attribution and quote-wording problems, not fabrications of the underlying events.
editor_notes.originality: Not a duplicate -- no prior coverage of this incident.
concerns: RPM remediation breakdown misattributed to BleepingComputer when it's actually from Mozilla's blog.
One quote ('implemented safeguards to prevent similar incidents') paraphrases Mozilla's actual wording while presented as verbatim.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Approve with corrections. The article is accurate; the misattribution and quote-fidelity issue are both isolated to subordinate claims and are honestly covered by a public corrections note.
